questions.q: Which three conversations does the summary say are happening at once in every hard exchange?
a: What happened, feelings, and identity
Facts, solutions, and apologies
Past, present, and future
Blame, compromise, and trust
questions.why: Lesson 1 breaks every difficult conversation into the What Happened, Feelings, and Identity conversations.

questions.q: In the What Happened conversation, what should replace assigning blame?
a: Looking at how everyone contributed to the problem
Agreeing on who was mostly at fault
Setting aside the facts until later
Letting the other person speak first
questions.why: Lesson 2 recommends dropping the blame game and examining how each side played a part.

questions.q: What does the summary mean by your emotional footprint?
a: The past experiences that shape how you react
The feelings you leave others with after a talk
The emotions you hide during a conflict
The tone of voice you use when upset
questions.why: Lesson 2 describes the emotional footprint as the reason behind your reactions, rooted in past experience.

questions.q: What advice does the summary give for handling the Identity conversation?
a: Remember that your identity has many components
Avoid discussing anything personal at work
Decide firmly whether you are kind or mean
Let the other person define who you are
questions.why: Lesson 2 warns against absolute labels for yourself and suggests seeing identity as made of many parts.

questions.q: How should a third story be told when opening a tricky conversation?
a: As an impartial observer of both sides
From your own point of view, clearly stated
Through a friend who speaks for you
As a list of complaints and fixes
questions.why: Lesson 3 says the third story belongs to neither side and is told like a neutral observer's account.
